clinicalPearls: A rare chronic non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis of adults presenting as indurated yellow to violaceous plaques and nodules that characteristically ulcerate and develop atrophic, telangiectatic centres.
The periorbital region is the most frequently affected site, though the trunk and limbs are also involved; periorbital disease may be complicated by ectropion, scarring and ocular inflammation.
A strong association with monoclonal gammopathy, most often IgG kappa, is a defining feature and may precede or follow the skin disease by years.
It is linked to underlying or subsequent lymphoproliferative and plasma cell disorders, including multiple myeloma and other B-cell dyscrasias, mandating long-term haematological surveillance.

Histology shows extensive palisading and diffuse xanthogranulomatous inflammation with broad zones of necrobiosis (hyaline collagen degeneration), numerous Touton and foreign-body giant cells and cholesterol clefts.
Cholesterol clefts and lymphoid aggregates within the necrobiotic zones help distinguish it from necrobiosis lipoidica and other palisading granulomas.
Complement abnormalities, cryoglobulinaemia and low C1 esterase inhibitor levels have been described in some patients.
Management is directed at the underlying paraproteinaemia; alkylating and other systemic immunomodulatory agents are used, and disfiguring or ulcerated lesions may require specialist care.
reference.pathophysiology: Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is a xanthogranulomatous histiocytic disorder in which lipid-laden macrophages, Touton and foreign-body giant cells accumulate within the dermis and subcutis, producing broad bands of collagen necrobiosis interspersed with cholesterol clefts and lymphoplasmacytic aggregates. Its consistent association with a monoclonal paraprotein, usually IgG kappa, has led to the hypothesis that circulating immunoglobulin, potentially acting as an antibody with lipoprotein-binding activity or forming immune complexes, drives a granulomatous foreign-body-type reaction to lipid within tissue. The resulting chronic granulomatous inflammation degrades dermal collagen and elastic tissue, giving the characteristic atrophic, telangiectatic and ulcerating plaques. The frequent coexistence of, or progression to, plasma cell and lymphoproliferative disorders underscores that the cutaneous disease is a marker of an underlying clonal immunoglobulin-producing process.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous involvement by lymphoma or plasma cell disorder
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with histology showing necrobiosis, cholesterol clefts and Touton giant cells
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation to detect a monoclonal paraprotein
Bone marrow examination when a plasma cell or lymphoproliferative disorder is suspected
Full blood count, renal profile and serum calcium as myeloma screen
Complement studies and cryoglobulins where indicated
Ophthalmological assessment for periorbital and ocular complications
redFlags: Detection of a monoclonal paraprotein or rising paraprotein level indicating an evolving plasma cell dyscrasia
Anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment or bone pain suggesting multiple myeloma
Periorbital ulceration, ectropion or ocular inflammation threatening vision
Lymphadenopathy or organomegaly suggesting lymphoproliferative disease
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous disease is chronic, progressive and relapsing, and while the skin lesions themselves are not life-threatening, prognosis is governed by the associated haematological disorder, which may evolve into multiple myeloma or lymphoma over many years and necessitates indefinite surveillance.
pitfalls: Confusing it histologically and clinically with necrobiosis lipoidica and missing the associated paraproteinaemia.
Failing to perform and repeat serum protein electrophoresis, since the gammopathy may appear years after the skin disease.
Attributing periorbital plaques to ordinary xanthelasma and overlooking the systemic implications.
Neglecting long-term haematological monitoring after an initially negative myeloma screen.
Aggressive surgery on ulceration-prone lesions that heal poorly and may recur.
